question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \iint\limits_{S} 12xyz \: \textrm{d}S \] where $S$ is defined by $z=x+y$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x+y) = 1, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(x+y) = 1. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S 12xyz \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, 12xy(x+y)\sqrt{1+1^2+1^2} \: \text{d}A\\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, 12xy(x+y)\sqrt{3} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt 3\iint\limits_D\, 12x^2y+12xy^2 \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{3} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} (12x^2y+12xy^2) \: \text{d}y \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{3} \int_{0}^{1} \big[ 6x^2y^2+4xy^3 \big]_{y=0}^{y=1} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{3} \int_{0}^{1} (6x^2+4x) \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{3} \, \big[ 2x^3+2x^2 \big]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{3} (2+2) - 0 \\[5pt] &= 4\sqrt{3} \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}( x^2+y^2) \: \textrm{d}S, \] where $S$ is defined by $z=2x-y$ and whose domain is the circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(2x-y) = 2, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(2x-y) = -1. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} ( x^2+y^2)\: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D ( x^2+y^2) \cdot \sqrt{1+2^2+(-1)^2}\, \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D ( x^2+y^2) \cdot \sqrt{6}\, \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{6} \iint\limits_D \,( x^2+y^2) \: \text{d}A. \end{align*}

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq {2\pi} \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

\begin{align} \sqrt{6} \iint\limits_D \,( x^2+y^2)\: \text{d}A & = \sqrt{6} \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \: r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta \\[5pt] & = \sqrt{6} \iint\limits_{\Delta}( r^2\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin^2\theta ) \cdot r \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & =\sqrt{6} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2} r^3 \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \sqrt{6} \int_0^{2\pi} \left[ \dfrac{r^4}4 \right]_{0}^{2} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \sqrt{6} \int_0^{2\pi} 4 \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & =4\sqrt{6} \int_0^{2\pi} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & =4\sqrt{6} \big[ {\theta} \big]_0^{2\pi} \\[5pt] & = 8{\sqrt{6}}\pi. \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} \sqrt{ x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}S, \] where $S$ is defined by $z=4x+\sqrt{8}y$ and whose domain is the circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(4x+\sqrt{8}y) = 4, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(4x+\sqrt{8}y) = \sqrt{8}. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S}\sqrt{ x^2+y^2}\: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{ x^2+y^2} \cdot \sqrt{1+4^2+(\sqrt{8})^2}\, \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{ x^2+y^2} \cdot 5\, \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= 5 \iint\limits_D \,\sqrt{ x^2+y^2} \: \text{d}A. \end{align*}

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq {2\pi} \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

\begin{align} 5 \iint\limits_D \,\sqrt{ x^2+y^2}\: \text{d}A & = 5 \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \: r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta \\[5pt] & = 5 \iint\limits_{\Delta}\sqrt{ r^2\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin^2\theta }\cdot r \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & =5 \int_0^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2} r^2 \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 5 \int_0^{2\pi} \left[ \dfrac{r^3}3 \right]_{0}^{2} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 5 \int_0^{2\pi} \dfrac{8}{3} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & =\dfrac{40}{3}\int_0^{2\pi} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & =\dfrac{40}{3} \big[ {\theta} \big]_0^{2\pi} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{80\pi }{3}. \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \iint\limits_{S} \sqrt z \: \textrm{d}S \] where $S$ is defined by $z=y-3x$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $3x \leq y \leq 3.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(y-3x) = -3, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(y-3x) = 1. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \sqrt z \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, \sqrt{y-3x}\sqrt{1+(-3)^2+1^2} \: \text{d}A\\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, \sqrt{y-3x}\sqrt{11} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{11}\iint\limits_D\,\sqrt{y-3x} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{11} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{3x}^{3} \sqrt{y-3x} \: \text{d}y \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{11} \int_{0}^{1} \left[ \dfrac 23 (y-3x)^{3/2} \right]_{y=3x}^{y=3} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{11}}3 \int_{0}^{1} (3-3x)^{3/2} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{11}}3 \, \left[ \dfrac 25 \cdot \left( -\dfrac 13\right)(3-3x)^{5/2} \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{4\sqrt{11}}{45} \left(0-3^{5/2}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4\sqrt{11}}{45} \left(9\sqrt{3}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4\sqrt{33}}{5} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \iint\limits_{S} z^2 \: \textrm{d}S \] where $S$ is defined by $z=e^x$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $x \leq y \leq x+1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(e^x) = e^x, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(e^x) = 0. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S z^2 \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, z^2 \sqrt{1+e^{2x}+0^2} \: \text{d}A\\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, e^{2x}\sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{x}^{x+1} e^{2x}\sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} \: \text{d}y \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left[ e^{2x}\sqrt{1 + e^{2x}}y \right]_{y=x}^{y=x+1} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 e^{2x}\sqrt{1 + e^{2x}} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac 13 (1 + e^{2x})^{3/2} \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 13 \left( (1+e^2)^{3/2} - 2^{3/2} \right) \end{align*}
